groups.label: Finding the pull back home
groups.summary: Questions in this family ask whether a motion is simple harmonic, or ask the solver to expose the proportional restoring relation that makes it so.
checks: Reduce a force law, acceleration relation, graph or physical arrangement to a quantity proportional to displacement and pointing back towards equilibrium; or identify exactly why that test fails.

groups.label: Reading an oscillator at an instant
groups.summary: Questions in this family ask what the oscillator is doing at one position or instant, rather than for a complete trace.
checks: Locate the oscillator within the cycle and infer the direction, sign, size or extremum of another motion quantity.

groups.label: Translating the cycle
groups.summary: Questions in this family ask for a change of representation while preserving the oscillator's phase, amplitude and timing.
checks: Translate among words, equations and graphs; use the initial condition to anchor phase; and keep track of quarter-cycle shifts and doubled energy frequency.

groups.label: Following the energy round the cycle
groups.summary: Questions in this family track total, kinetic, elastic and gravitational energy through an oscillation.
checks: Fix the constant total energy, allocate it between stores at a stated displacement or time, and use the allocation to recover speed, position or scale changes.

groups.label: Building an oscillator's clock
groups.summary: Questions in this family construct or compare the timing law of a pendulum, mass–spring system or less familiar oscillator.
checks: Identify the effective inertia and restoring stiffness, obtain an angular frequency or period, and then compare, infer or design around it.

groups.label: Watching the motion die away
groups.summary: Questions in this family concern free oscillations whose mechanical energy is being removed.
checks: Read or predict a decay envelope, connect amplitude loss to energy loss and quality factor, or distinguish the limiting damping regimes.

groups.label: Pushing at the right rhythm
groups.summary: Questions in this family concern the response of an oscillator to a periodic driver.
checks: Compare forcing and natural frequencies, read the amplitude and phase response, and reason about damping, energy input and resonance risk.

groups.label: Making the oscillator answer an experiment
groups.summary: Questions in this family use oscillations as a measurement method or ask the solver to design, analyse or critique an oscillator experiment.
checks: Turn repeated cycles into a stable measurement, choose a linear plot, extract a parameter and account for uncertainty and controls.

groups.label: Finding where the idealisation breaks
groups.summary: Questions in this family probe the approximation that makes a real oscillator harmonic.
checks: Identify the small parameter, compare the exact and linearised restoring relations, and predict the consequences of nonlinearity.

atoms.label: State the two defining conditions for SHM
atoms.summary: The command is state, describe or outline the conditions for SHM, with no physical derivation requested.
checks: State that acceleration (or resultant force) is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed oppositely. Include both proportionality and restoring direction.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: A bare definition prompt; an oscillator introduced before later calculations.
atoms.authored_shape: State the proportional-and-opposite restoring condition.

atoms.label: Recognise the SHM restoring graph or relation
atoms.summary: Several F–x or a–x relations are offered and only one is a straight line through the origin with negative gradient.
checks: Test linearity through equilibrium and the negative sign. Reject any curve, offset or positive gradient that breaks F∝–x or a∝–x.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Multiple-choice force–displacement graphs; acceleration–displacement plots; a stated restoring-force rule.
atoms.authored_shape: Recognise SHM from a force/acceleration–displacement relation.

atoms.label: Decide that a proposed motion is not exact SHM
atoms.summary: The question asks whether a motion is SHM after presenting a non-linear or otherwise imperfect restoring model.
checks: Inspect the restoring relation over the stated range. It is exact SHM only if the force or acceleration remains proportional to –x; otherwise state the limited range, if any, where the approximation works.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Competing spring models; unfamiliar force curves; large-displacement motion.
atoms.authored_shape: Reject motion whose restoring relation is wrong.

atoms.label: Show that a physical setup produces SHM
atoms.summary: A real setup is displaced slightly and the command asks why it oscillates simply harmonically.
checks: Find the change in resultant force caused by a displacement, show it is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it, then connect ma=–Kx to a=–ω²x.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Floating cork or ball; spring systems; charge or mass arrangements; buoyancy oscillators.
atoms.authored_shape: Justify SHM from the forces in a physical setup.

atoms.label: Extract angular frequency, frequency or period from an a–x gradient
atoms.summary: A straight acceleration–displacement graph is supplied and a frequency or period is requested.
checks: Use gradient=–ω², take the positive square root for ω, and convert with f=ω/(2π) or T=2π/ω. Keep graph units in SI.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Generic particle; LP-record stylus; mass–spring oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Extract angular frequency or period from the slope of an acceleration–displacement graph.

atoms.label: Explain why the SHM approximation is useful
atoms.summary: The prompt acknowledges that real oscillations are not exactly SHM and asks why the model is still studied.
checks: Say that many stable systems have an approximately linear restoring force for small displacements, so the solvable SHM model predicts their leading behaviour and provides a baseline for non-linearity and damping.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: General modelling or engineering context.
atoms.authored_shape: Explain why SHM is useful as a small-oscillation approximation.

atoms.label: Read amplitude from a trace or extreme separation
atoms.summary: A displacement trace or pair of extreme positions is shown and the amplitude is requested or embedded in a multiple-choice pair.
checks: Locate equilibrium, measure the maximum displacement from it, and do not confuse amplitude with peak-to-peak distance. Convert the graph scale before reporting the value.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Generic oscillator trace; local particle in a travelling wave; diagram with two turning points.
atoms.authored_shape: Define amplitude as the maximum displacement from equilibrium.

atoms.label: Locate the true equilibrium position
atoms.summary: A physical oscillator has a geometrically central-looking point, but equilibrium must be located from zero resultant force or the displaced spring length.
checks: Set the resultant force to zero, not each force separately. For a vertical spring use kx=mg to find the equilibrium extension before measuring displacement about it.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum; vertically loaded spring; floating object; asymmetric-looking oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Identify the equilibrium position in a physical oscillator, rather than assuming that every central-looking point is equilibrium.

atoms.label: Relate the signs, zeros and extrema of x, v and a
atoms.summary: One motion quantity is zero or at an extremum and the signs or values of the other two are requested.
checks: Use a=–ω²x and the cycle landmarks: at equilibrium x=a=0 and |v| is maximum; at either extreme v=0 and |a| is maximum, directed inward.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Bare SHM particle; pendulum; mass–spring oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Relate the signs, zeros and extrema of displacement, velocity and acceleration.

atoms.label: Infer direction of motion at a stated instant
atoms.summary: A point on a trace, an energy graph, or a phase relation is supplied and an arrow or direction is requested.
checks: Identify whether displacement is increasing or decreasing at that instant. Use the trace slope, the sign of v, or the stated phase relation; do not use the acceleration direction as the velocity direction.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Particle trace; driven mass; vertical magnet–spring system; local wave particle.
atoms.authored_shape: Find the direction of motion at an instant.

atoms.label: Calculate instantaneous speed from displacement
atoms.summary: Amplitude, angular frequency or period, and the present displacement are known; the speed away from a landmark is requested.
checks: Find ω if needed, then use |v|=ω√(x₀²–x²). Determine the sign separately from direction information; the square-root relation gives speed only.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Bare oscillator; iceberg; mass on a spring; plate vibration.
atoms.authored_shape: Calculate instantaneous speed from displacement.

atoms.label: Calculate maximum speed from amplitude and timing
atoms.summary: Amplitude and f, T or ω are given, and the speed at equilibrium or the maximum speed is requested.
checks: Convert the timing data to ω and use vₘₐₓ=ωx₀. Check that the supplied distance is amplitude rather than total excursion.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Oscillating plate; pendulum bob; magnet–spring; local point in a vibrating medium.
atoms.authored_shape: Calculate maximum speed, maximum acceleration or maximum restoring force.

atoms.label: Calculate maximum acceleration or restoring force
atoms.summary: The question asks for the largest acceleration or spring force and gives amplitude plus timing or stiffness data.
checks: At an extreme use |a|max=ω²x₀, then Fmax=m|a|max or kx₀ as appropriate. Keep the restoring direction separate from the requested magnitude.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Mass–spring oscillator; vibrating point; pendulum at small angle.
atoms.authored_shape: Calculate maximum speed, maximum acceleration or maximum restoring force.

atoms.label: Find average speed over a complete cycle
atoms.summary: Average speed is requested for one complete oscillation and amplitude and frequency or period are given.
checks: Use total distance 4x₀ per cycle and divide by T, giving average speed 4x₀/T=4fx₀. Do not average the signed velocity.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Bare SHM particle or mass–spring oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Find average speed over one cycle.

atoms.label: Count equal-energy or repeated-condition instants
atoms.summary: The question asks how many times per cycle two energies or oscillator quantities are equal.
checks: Solve the condition within one quarter-cycle, then use symmetry to count its repeated occurrence across all four quarters. Do not count the start again at the end of the same cycle.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum; horizontal spring; energy partition over a cycle.
atoms.authored_shape: Identify repeated instants at which two oscillator quantities meet a stated condition.

atoms.label: Convert cycle fractions into elapsed or repeat times

atoms.label: Convert among x-, v- and a-time graphs

atoms.authored_shape: Convert between displacement-, velocity- and acceleration-time graphs.

atoms.label: Match a displacement description to its velocity equation
atoms.summary: A displacement trace or expression is followed by several candidate velocity expressions.
checks: Differentiate the displacement expression, carrying the ω amplitude factor and the sine/cosine sign change. Test the result at one known turning point or equilibrium crossing.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Vertical spring; bare particle; oscillator described by a sinusoidal displacement.
atoms.authored_shape: Convert between displacement-, velocity- and acceleration equations.

atoms.label: Choose the sine/cosine sign from the initial condition
atoms.summary: The oscillator starts at a named extreme or equilibrium crossing and candidate sinusoidal functions differ only by sine/cosine and sign.
checks: Evaluate x and v at t=0 for each candidate, then use the initial direction to fix the remaining sign. A start at an extreme needs cosine-type displacement; a start at equilibrium needs sine-type displacement.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Iceberg released at its lowest point; mass released from a negative displacement; generic particle at t=0.
atoms.authored_shape: Choose a sine/cosine expression and sign from the initial condition.

atoms.label: Draw a motion trace with numerical phase and scale
atoms.summary: A blank set of time axes is supplied and the requested x, v or a curve must carry correct amplitude, period and starting phase.
checks: Calculate the plotted quantity's amplitude and period first, mark quarter-cycle landmarks, then draw one smooth sinusoid through them with the initial sign and direction fixed.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Buoyancy oscillator; mass–spring; pendulum; vibrating point.
atoms.authored_shape: Draw a requested motion graph with the right phase, amplitude and period.

atoms.label: Read period, frequency and amplitude from an oscillation trace
atoms.summary: A displacement–time trace is presented and the answer choices pair a timing quantity with amplitude.
checks: Measure one complete repeat for T, invert for f, and read amplitude from equilibrium to an extreme. Do not use peak-to-peak time or height as T or amplitude.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Local particle in a medium; generic oscillator; wave-driven particle kept as a shared C.1 part.
atoms.authored_shape: Read period, frequency and amplitude from an oscillation trace.

atoms.label: Draw a second oscillator with a stated phase lead or lag
atoms.summary: A reference trace and a phase difference between two oscillators or neighbouring particles are given.
checks: Convert the phase difference to a horizontal shift Δt=(Δφ/2π)T, preserve period and specified amplitude, and shift in the correct lead/lag direction.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Two particles P and Q; neighbouring atoms; two independent oscillators.
atoms.authored_shape: Draw a second oscillator trace with a stated phase lead or lag.

atoms.label: Recover amplitude from area under a quarter-cycle v–t graph
atoms.summary: A velocity–time trace is supplied, amplitude is requested, and the interval spans a turning point to equilibrium or one quarter-cycle.
checks: Use displacement=area under the v–t graph. The magnitude of the area over a turning-point-to-equilibrium quarter-cycle is exactly the amplitude; evaluate the sinusoidal area or the graph's stated scale.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Legacy generic-particle velocity trace.
atoms.authored_shape: Recover the amplitude from the area under a velocity–time graph over a quarter-cycle. [legacy-only candidate]

atoms.label: Describe the energy exchange through one cycle
atoms.summary: The command is describe or narrate energy changes rather than calculate a numerical energy.
checks: Track kinetic and potential stores at equilibrium, extremes and intermediate motion. State that total mechanical energy stays constant when damping is absent and reverse the transfer after each turning point.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum; spring–mass; satellite and tether; undamped generic oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Narrate energy exchange through successive fractional cycles.

atoms.label: Recognise or draw energy–time graphs
atoms.summary: Kinetic, potential or total energy is plotted against time for an undamped oscillator.
checks: Square the underlying sinusoid for KE or PE: values stay non-negative and repeat every T/2. Place maxima at equilibrium for KE and at extremes for PE; total energy is constant.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Generic particle; spring–mass; cylinder; pendulum.
atoms.authored_shape: Draw kinetic-, potential- or total-energy variation against time or displacement.

atoms.label: Recognise or draw energy–displacement graphs
atoms.summary: Potential, kinetic or total energy is plotted against displacement rather than time.
checks: Draw PE as an upward symmetric curve about equilibrium, total energy as a horizontal cap, and KE as the difference. Mark turning points where KE reaches zero.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Horizontal spring; generic SHM energy diagram; non-linear comparison model.
atoms.authored_shape: Draw kinetic-, potential- or total-energy variation against time or displacement.

atoms.label: Calculate total oscillation energy from amplitude
atoms.summary: Amplitude plus m and ω, or spring stiffness k, are given and the constant total energy is requested.
checks: Use Eᴛ=½mω²x₀² or, for a spring, Eᴛ=½kx₀². Convert peak-to-peak distance to amplitude and calculate ω from T or f when necessary.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Wooden block on a spring; generic body; plate, magnet or loudspeaker component.
atoms.authored_shape: Calculate total energy from amplitude and either stiffness or mass and angular frequency.

atoms.label: Derive the total-energy expression from the turning point
atoms.summary: The command is show that or derive, and the target is Eᴛ in terms of k and amplitude rather than a numerical result.
checks: Evaluate the motion at a turning point where v=0, so all mechanical energy is elastic potential energy. Substitute x=x₀ into ½kx² and identify that value with the constant total energy.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Compressed spring released from rest.
atoms.authored_shape: Derive or use the equality of total energy and maximum elastic potential energy.

atoms.label: Find kinetic or potential energy at a stated displacement
atoms.summary: Total energy and displacement as a fraction of amplitude are given; one energy store is requested.
checks: Use PE/Eᴛ=x²/x₀² and KE=Eᴛ–PE. Square the displacement fraction before subtracting; the sign of displacement does not change the energy.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Bare SHM particle; pendulum; horizontal spring.
atoms.authored_shape: Split total energy into kinetic and potential parts at a stated displacement.

atoms.label: Recover displacement or speed from an energy condition
atoms.summary: An energy fraction, equal-energy condition or marked energy graph is given and position or speed is requested.
checks: Express the stated energy as a fraction of Eᴛ, solve x²/x₀²=PE/Eᴛ for |x|, or use KE=½mv². Apply the graph's phase or direction only after finding the magnitude.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum energy trace; spring with KE=PE; unknown position on an energy curve.
atoms.authored_shape: Infer displacement or speed from an energy fraction or graph.

atoms.label: Scale oscillation energy after a parameter change
atoms.summary: Mass, stiffness, amplitude, frequency or period changes and the new total or maximum potential energy is requested as a ratio.
checks: Choose Eᴛ∝kx₀² or Eᴛ∝mω²x₀² and form a ratio before substituting. Do not introduce mass into ½kx₀² when k and amplitude alone fix the energy.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Loaded spring; altered mass and amplitude; same oscillator in a second trial.
atoms.authored_shape: Scale energy when amplitude, mass, stiffness, frequency or period changes.

atoms.label: Decode a vertical spring's elastic-energy trace
atoms.summary: Elastic potential energy of a vertical spring is plotted against time and does not vanish at the oscillator's equilibrium position.
checks: First find the equilibrium extension from kx=mg. Convert each elastic-energy level through Eₚ=½kx² to spring extension, then measure the oscillation amplitude about the equilibrium extension and combine with total-energy conservation as required.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Magnet or mass on a vertical spring that remains stretched throughout the motion.
atoms.authored_shape: Handle gravitational and elastic energy together in a vertical oscillator.

atoms.label: Scale pendulum period, frequency or angular frequency
atoms.summary: Length, gravitational field or bob mass changes and the new T, f or ω is requested as a ratio.
checks: Use T∝√(l/g), f∝√(g/l), or ω∝√(g/l). Cancel bob mass explicitly and square the given factor only inside the square-root relationship.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Earth, Moon or Mercury; changed pendulum length; changed bob mass as a distractor.
atoms.authored_shape: Scale a simple-pendulum period or frequency with length and gravitational field, recognising mass independence.

atoms.label: Scale mass–spring period or frequency
atoms.summary: Mass or spring stiffness changes while the other remains fixed and a period/frequency ratio is requested.
checks: Use T∝√(m/k) or f∝√(k/m), form new/old ratios, and ignore amplitude and gravitational field unless they change the effective stiffness.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Two spring trials; changed attached mass; same spring in a different gravitational field.
atoms.authored_shape: Scale a mass–spring period or frequency with mass and stiffness, recognising gravitational-field independence.

atoms.label: Find effective stiffness before finding the period
atoms.summary: More than one spring acts on the same mass and the new period is requested.
checks: Displace the mass and add the restoring-force contributions to obtain k_eff. Then use T=2π√(m/k_eff); do not combine springs by circuit rules without checking the geometry.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Identical parallel springs; mass between two springs; altered spring arrangement.
atoms.authored_shape: Combine springs to obtain an effective stiffness and period.

atoms.label: Infer an unknown mass or stiffness from period data
atoms.summary: Two periods, masses or force constants are compared and one oscillator parameter is unknown.
checks: Write T²∝m/k for each case, take a ratio to cancel the unchanged quantity, and solve for the unknown. If force–extension data are supplied, find k before applying the period law.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Known calibration mass and unknown wooden block; two spring models; cable treated as a spring.
atoms.authored_shape: Infer an unknown mass or stiffness from period data.

atoms.label: Build a period law from an unfamiliar restoring force
atoms.summary: A non-standard oscillator is described by forces or a graph and its period must be shown, calculated or compared.
checks: Linearise the resultant force about equilibrium to F≈–Kx, identify ω²=K/m, and use T=2π/ω. State the small-displacement assumption that makes K constant.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Buoyant ball; charged or gravitating masses; non-linear spring model in the small-displacement limit.
atoms.authored_shape: Model a non-standard oscillator from its restoring law.

atoms.label: Compare unlike oscillators after the same change
atoms.summary: A pendulum and mass–spring system undergo the same change in mass, gravity or environment and their periods must be compared.
checks: Write each system's own period law separately, cancel variables that do not appear, then compare the two ratios. Do not transfer the pendulum's g-dependence to the spring system.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Earth-to-Moon comparison; simultaneous changes to pendulum bob and spring mass.
atoms.authored_shape: Compare two oscillator designs or environments through their period laws.

atoms.label: Combine unequal fractional-cycle times in a piecewise pendulum
atoms.summary: A pendulum changes effective length part-way through each swing and one complete period must be assembled.
checks: Treat each arc as a quarter-cycle of the appropriate simple-pendulum period, count how many quarters use each length, and add them before simplifying.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum string catching on a peg; two effective lengths on opposite sides.
atoms.authored_shape: Combine the times for different fractional cycles in a piecewise pendulum. [legacy-only candidate]

atoms.label: Time many oscillations to reduce timing uncertainty
atoms.summary: The method times 20 or another large number of cycles and asks why this improves T or what uncertainty to quote.
checks: The absolute start/stop reaction-time uncertainty is spread over many periods; divide the total time and its absolute uncertainty by the number of cycles. Use repeats to estimate random spread separately.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum timing; suspended rod; repeated manual stopwatch measurements.
atoms.authored_shape: Time many cycles to reduce relative timing uncertainty.

atoms.label: Choose a linear plot to test an oscillator model
atoms.summary: A proposed period relationship is given and the axes or transformed variable for a straight-line graph must be chosen.
checks: Rearrange the proposed law into y=mx+c, choose the squared or reciprocal variables that make it linear, and use intercept behaviour as part of the model test.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum T versus L; suspended rod; unfamiliar oscillator with a power-law hypothesis.
atoms.authored_shape: Linearise and test an oscillator relationship.

atoms.label: Extract a physical parameter from gradient or intercept
atoms.summary: A best-fit line from oscillator data is supplied and g, stiffness, a model constant or an effective length is requested.
checks: Match the fitted gradient/intercept to the rearranged theoretical coefficient, include graph-axis multipliers and units, then solve for the physical parameter rather than reporting the raw gradient alone.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum linearisation; suspended rod; mass–spring model.
atoms.authored_shape: Obtain a physical parameter from a graph gradient or intercept.

atoms.label: Choose controls and diagnose the dominant timing error
atoms.summary: A pendulum or oscillator investigation asks for a controlled variable or the main source of error in T.
checks: Hold fixed every factor in the period law except the independent variable, and name a timing error that changes the measured interval, such as reaction time or inconsistent release/detection—not a vague 'human error'.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Pendulum length investigation; mass or separation varied in a physical oscillator.
atoms.authored_shape: Choose controls and identify the dominant timing error.

atoms.label: Propagate uncertainty through an oscillator result
atoms.summary: Measured T and length or a percentage uncertainty are given, and g or another derived oscillator parameter must include an uncertainty.
checks: Rearrange the period law for the target, multiply each fractional uncertainty by its power, add worst-case fractional contributions, then round the absolute uncertainty before matching the value's decimal place.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Simple-pendulum determination of g; graph-derived result; period-versus-speed experiment.
atoms.authored_shape: Propagate or estimate uncertainty in an oscillator measurement.

atoms.label: Use oscillator cycles as a clock for another motion
atoms.summary: A periodic pen, marker or oscillator trace records equal time intervals while a cart or other body moves.

atoms.authored_shape: Use a periodic marker as a clock for another motion.

atoms.label: Determine the valid small-amplitude range of a pendulum model
atoms.summary: Period data are plotted against release angle and a tolerance for treating T as amplitude-independent is supplied.
checks: Calculate or read the fractional change from the small-angle period, compare it with the stated tolerance, and identify the largest angle still inside the acceptable band.
atoms.authored_typical_setups: Simple pendulum released from progressively larger angles.
atoms.authored_shape: Test the small-amplitude limit of a pendulum or other oscillator.

atoms.label: Predict how nonlinearity changes the period
atoms.summary: A restoring-force model departs from its small-displacement straight line and the large-amplitude period change is requested without calculation.

atoms.authored_shape: Predict how a nonlinear restoring law changes period.

atoms.label: Infer a non-linear potential-energy curve from the restoring force

checks: Use F=–dEₚ/dx qualitatively: the force magnitude is the slope magnitude of the energy curve. Compare steepness and curvature with the linear-spring parabola while keeping a minimum at equilibrium.

atoms.authored_shape: Predict how a nonlinear restoring law changes potential energy.

atoms.label: Use Q to connect stored energy, cycle loss, amplitude decay and power

C1-1.1.marks: Usually 2 marks: one for acceleration (or force) proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, one for directed towards equilibrium, or opposite to the displacement. Where the stem names a body, the marker wants it clear what is accelerating: no named body, 1 max (M13). 'Directed towards the centre' was refused in N13; say the equilibrium position. 'From equilibrium' is sometimes where the first mark hangs.
C1-1.1.note: (a ∝ -x and F ∝ -x are the same statement; either earns the mark if the words say what the sign means.)

C1-1.2.marks: 1 mark. Any of: obeys Hooke's law, has a fixed spring constant, force proportional to displacement (N25 SL). A consequence of SHM (constant period, period independent of amplitude) does not earn it; neither does 'no energy loss'.

C1-1.3.marks: Recognition is 1 mark. Explanation is 2 to 4: proportional (straight line through the origin) and opposite direction (negative gradient), with the feature and the conclusion each earning separately when 4 are available (M09, M14). 'Centre' or 'fixed point' for equilibrium was refused in M14.

C1-1.4.marks: 1 mark. Straight, through the origin, negative gradient. The positive-gradient line and the curve through the origin are the distractors that work.

C1-1.5.marks: 2 marks when asked (M11 HL, the U-tube with a = -(2g/l)x: explain, with reference to the motion of the liquid, the significance of the negative sign): the acceleration is always directed towards equilibrium, or opposite to the displacement, and the motion is therefore simple harmonic. A statement that the acceleration is negative earns nothing.
C1-1.5.note: (The share reads zero because the 6 September counting workbook does not carry that U-tube subpart as an item; the pack has it. Adding it moves every denominator by one.)

C1-1.6.marks: Both halves, explicitly: proportional to displacement and opposite in direction. When the question supplies the law, the marks are for reading the two properties off it, not for repeating the law. M18 HL gave 1 mark for proportionality alone and said direction was not required; that is the exception, not the rule.

C1-1.7.marks: Typically 2 marks (M25, both levels, the cork): one for the physical origin of the extra force (upthrust exceeds weight, or upthrust grows with submersion), one for proportional and opposite, with 'quotes a = -ω²x' accepted for the second. The mark most often lost is the first: candidates state the SHM condition without saying where the restoring force comes from.
C1-1.7.note: (Floating body: extra upthrust ρgAx. Two springs on one coordinate: k₁ + k₂. Bowl: the tangential component of weight. Charge: the local force gradient.)

C1-1.8.marks: 1 mark per direction (M25 SL, two charges). The mark is for the direction of the net force after displacement and the motion that follows; 'zero force at the point' earns nothing on its own. Stable in one direction and unstable in the other is the intended answer.

C1-1.9.marks: Not seen as a direct target in the corpus. When it appears it is the curve option on a graph pick, or the 'only for small amplitude' qualifier in an explanation.

C1-1.10.marks: 1 mark for the relevant condition: small angle so sin θ ≈ θ; small displacement compared with the geometry; the spring within its Hooke's-law range. A generic 'no friction' is not the condition asked for unless the stem is about energy.

C1-2.1.marks: At +A and -A: v = 0, |a| maximum, KE zero, PE maximum. At equilibrium: |v| maximum, a = 0, KE maximum, PE minimum. In between: all intermediate.

C1-2.2.marks: 1 mark each. Speed and KE maximum at equilibrium, zero at the extremes; acceleration, force and PE the other way round. On the school's own tests the working distractors are 'halfway out' for maximum speed and the extremes for zero acceleration.

C1-2.3.marks: 1 mark. The mark hangs on reading the convention off the figure; equilibrium is often not at the geometric origin or the natural length.

C1-2.4.marks: 1 mark. From an x-t graph the gradient decides; from a v-x graph the branch; from a diagram the elapsed fraction of a period. A positive displacement is not a positive velocity, and that confusion is what the distractors are built on.

C1-2.5.marks: 1 mark. Towards equilibrium, always; opposite to x. On a labelled x-t graph the point at maximum displacement is the point of maximum acceleration, and it points back.

C1-2.6.marks: 1 mark. Same sign for v and a means speeding up, which is the inbound half of every swing. On the school's tests the inbound-and-slowing answer takes as many candidates as the right one.

C1-2.7.marks: 1 mark; the answer is a half for both. A quarter is the common wrong answer. Energy conditions need the displacement boundary found first and then mapped onto the cycle.

C1-2.8.marks: 1 mark, often multi-select. v = 0 with |a| maximum: yes, at an extreme. a = 0 with KE maximum: yes, at equilibrium. x = 0 with v = 0, or a = 0 with KE = 0: impossible for any oscillation of non-zero amplitude.

C1-2.9.marks: 1 mark per correctly placed label; no partial credit for a label on the wrong branch. Counts: a signed value twice per cycle, a magnitude four times, an energy condition four times (because it depends on x²).

C1-3.1.marks: 1 mark. At T/4 equilibrium moving negative, at T/2 the other extreme, at 3T/4 equilibrium moving positive, at T the start. The trap that fires is linear-in-time reasoning, which puts the oscillator halfway out after a quarter period.

C1-3.2.marks: 1 mark. T/4, and the direction of the initial velocity decides which extreme. Where T/4 is not offered, 3T/4 is the first offered time at an extreme (the school's C1C2C5 Q2, 77 per cent right).

C1-3.3.marks: 1 mark. The same displacement with the same velocity needs a full period; the same displacement with the opposite velocity comes earlier, and T is the answer the marker is waiting to refuse.

C1-3.4.marks: 1 or 2 marks. The initial state is the whole question; a candidate who assumes a release from rest when the stem says through equilibrium loses everything.

C1-3.5.marks: 1 mark. Two, four, four. A candidate who has learnt the state table but not the cycle answers two to everything.

C1-3.6.marks: 1 mark: 4A, 4A/T, zero. On the school's C1C2C5 the item sits beside a displacement-distance graph and three fifths of candidates returned the wave speed λ/T; when the stem says 'a particle in the medium', the marker is looking for 4A/T.

C1-3.7.marks: 2 marks (N25 1B): one for identifying the number of periods (or T = 1/f), one for the time. Δt = n/f, and the unit was not required there.

C1-3.8.marks: 1 mark. KE and the SHM potential repeat every T/2, so double the energy repeat. A candidate who knows the doubling and then doubles again is a real, evidenced answer (4 s for 2 s on the school's item).

C1-3.9.marks: 1 mark, rare, and no longer syllabus content beyond the linking question. Δφ = 2πΔt/T is the whole of it.

C1-4.1.marks: 1 mark. From equilibrium to an extreme, never the full swing. Where the graph is a hanging spring, the equilibrium line is not the natural-length line, and the mark hangs on that.

C1-4.2.marks: The A = b/2 step is not marked on its own; it is the step before the formula, and the N25 HL item (speed at b/4) lost candidates at the translation rather than at the physics.

C1-4.3.marks: 1 mark. Between two identical states: consecutive maxima, or zero crossings in the same direction. Extreme to extreme is T/2, and reading T off a two-cycle graph as a single cycle is the other way to lose it.

C1-4.4.marks: 1 mark. f = 1/T and ω = 2πf. The 2π is the mark: ω = 2πT and f = T are the recorded wrong answers. Head work, no calculator needed.

C1-4.5.marks: 1 mark each. ω is the coefficient of t, whatever the equation looks like; T = 2π/ω. Units of t and the sine or cosine form do not change the reading.

C1-4.6.marks: 1 or 2 marks. The energy repeat is T/2; double it before it goes into any formula. This is the usual first step of a pendulum-length question and the usual place it is lost.

C1-4.7.marks: 1 mark (N25 SL 1A). f² = -gradient/(4π²), and stop there. The marker will not give the mark to f; the whole point of the item is the requested variable.

C1-4.8.marks: 1 or 2 marks. ω = a_max/v_max, then T = 2π/ω; A = v_max²/a_max. The school's Mini-Test item was answered correctly by under half.

C1-4.9.marks: Marks in comparison questions go to the proportional relation written down, then the factor. Working through two full calculations gets the same marks slower and loses them more often on the 2π and the units.

C1-5.1.marks: 1 or 2 marks: sine or negative sine curve, correct phase relative to x, same period (M10, M12). Amplitude is usually not marked. v is zero where x is at an extreme and maximum where x crosses zero; a copied x-t outline is the distractor that takes candidates.

C1-5.2.marks: 2 marks (N09): cosine shape with the same period; negative cosine. Amplitudes need not match. The mark most often lost is the sign.

C1-5.3.marks: 1 or 2 marks: same period and zero crossings, opposite sign. The in-phase copy is the working distractor.

C1-5.4.marks: 1 mark. Both the derivative relationship (v leads x by a quarter cycle) and the x-a inversion have to be right at once, which is why it is a good multiple-choice item.

C1-5.5.marks: 1 mark: area under v-t is displacement over the interval (signed), gradient of x-t is velocity. The Mini-Test area item (amplitude P) was answered correctly by under half.

C1-5.6.marks: 1 or 2 marks (M12): positive (or negative) sine graph, drawn correctly for one period. The initial state fixes the start: released from +A means x at a maximum with zero gradient; through equilibrium moving positively means x at zero with positive gradient.

C1-5.7.marks: Rarely a direct target. Where it is, the marks are for the time scale changing with frequency and the v and a amplitudes scaling with ω and ω².

C1-6.1.marks: Sketch: 1 or 2 marks for a straight line through the origin with negative gradient. Reading: the gradient is -ω², and see 7.4 for the chain that follows, because that is where the marks are lost.

C1-6.2.marks: 1 mark for the line; for a spring the gradient is -k. The same shape as 6.1 with the mass in the way.

C1-6.3.marks: 1 mark. An ellipse (or circle), not a sinusoid. Intercepts ±A on the x axis and ±v_max on the v axis; the upper branch is positive velocity. A sine drawn on these axes is the examiner's stock wrong answer.

C1-6.4.marks: 1 mark. The upper half of the ellipse: zero at ±A, maximum at x = 0. Not a straight line and not a sinusoid.

C1-6.5.marks: 1 or 2 marks: an upward parabola with its minimum at equilibrium, and a flat total-energy line touching it at ±A. The school's C1C2C5 item on this (Q20) is the one energy graph nearly everyone gets right.

C1-6.6.marks: 1 or 2 marks: a downward parabola over -A to +A, zeros at the extremes, maximum at equilibrium. For a second amplitude the maximum scales with A².

C1-6.7.marks: 1 mark per label. Horizontal extent is the amplitude, vertical intercept is a_max, v_max or KE_max according to the graph.

C1-6.8.marks: See 12.2, where the marks are. The trace is not an x-t graph: its horizontal axis is distance travelled, and the widening spacing is the cart speeding up, not the period changing.

C1-7.1.marks: 1 or 2 marks. a = -ω²x; the direction mark is separate and is for 'towards equilibrium', or the sign read correctly against the stated axis.

C1-7.2.marks: 1 mark. a ∝ x, so a₂/a₁ = x₂/x₁. Inverting the ratio is the recorded slip.

C1-7.3.marks: 2 marks (M15): one for ω (with the 2π), one for a_max = ω²A. F_max = ma_max, or kA for a spring measured from equilibrium. Bald correct answers usually earn full marks.

C1-7.4.marks: 3 or 4 marks (M09, M12): use of ω² = -a/x (or gradient), the value of ω², ω = 2πf, the answer. The heaviest single loss in the school's own data (38 of 46 on a four-marker; 12 of 15 on the Mini-Test), and on the Mini-Test the dominant error was a centimetre axis never converted, not the square root or the 2π.

C1-7.5.marks: 1 mark (N25 SL 1A). The item is designed around the coefficient: f² = -gradient/(4π²). Stop at f².

C1-7.6.marks: 2 or 3 marks (M11, M12): comparison with a = -ω²x to read ω² off, then T = 2π/ω, then the number. The second heaviest loss in the school's data: 42 of 47 lost marks, mostly by reaching for T = 2π√(m/k) from memory instead of reading the constant they had just been given.

C1-7.7.marks: Marked as part of the derivation. The examiner's line is that a show-that needs the physical bridge, not the quoted result.

C1-7.8.marks: Marks per stage, usually 1 each, with ECF. In a multi-stage item the stage most often lost is the first, establishing the force law.

C1-8A.1.marks: 1 or 2 marks. T = 2π√(m/k); a 2π dropped or a root missed is the whole loss.

C1-8A.2.marks: 1 mark (N25 SL, with a second for the Hooke's-law property): f ∝ 1/√m, so f/√3. The wrong answers that fire are the root missed and the direction inverted.

C1-8A.3.marks: 1 mark. k doubles and m doubles, so T is unchanged. On the school's C1C2C5 Q5, 12 of 30 changed the stiffness and forgot the mass, giving T/√2. That is the distractor to author.

C1-8A.4.marks: 1 mark. Unchanged, both. For the vertical spring g sets the equilibrium extension, not the period. 'Depends on g' takes 6 of 15 on the Mini-Test.

C1-8A.5.marks: 1 or 2 marks: T² = 4π²m/k, rearranged. Comparison versions use T₁²/T₂² = m₁/m₂ and the marker wants the squares.

C1-8B.1.marks: 1 or 2 marks. T = 2π√(L/g); the same losses as 8A.1.

C1-8B.2.marks: 1 mark. T ∝ √L and T ∝ 1/√g; the bob's mass does nothing. The Moon item is the one ratio the school's candidates can do (79 per cent); the halved-length item is the one they cannot, and the modal wrong answer takes the root correctly and inverts the direction (f/√2 for √2 f).

C1-8B.3.marks: 1 mark. Effective length is pivot to centre of mass; a shorter effective length gives a shorter period.

C1-8B.4.marks: 1 or 2 marks: L = gT²/(4π²). Where T comes from a KE graph, the energy period has to be doubled first (see 4.6), and that is the mark that goes.

C1-8C.marks: 1 mark. Mass changes the spring and not the pendulum; g changes the pendulum and not the spring; amplitude changes neither.

C1-9.1.marks: 2 or 3 marks (M12, M13): ω from T or f (with the 2π), then v_max = ωA. Where the amplitude is given as a full swing (A to B is 0.040 m), halving it is a mark in itself.

C1-9.2.marks: 1 or 2 marks: v = ω√(A² - x²). The direction is not determined by the displacement and is not asked for here.

C1-9.3.marks: 1 mark: (√3/2)v_max. v_max/2 is the modal wrong answer on the school's Mini-Test (6 of 15), and it is the same linear-interpolation error as E/2 in 10A.5.

C1-9.4.marks: 1 mark (N25 HL). Two inequalities at once: U/E = 1/4 is less than a half, v/v_max = √3/2 is greater than a half. The pair is the point; a candidate who assumes both scale the same way gets both wrong.

C1-9.5.marks: 1 or 2 marks: |x| = A√(1 - v²/v_max²), giving two positions unless a direction or time condition selects one.

C1-9.6.marks: 1 mark for the sign, from the branch: initial condition, graph gradient, phase, or whether it is moving towards or away from equilibrium.

C1-9.7.marks: 1 mark (N25 HL). A = b/2 and |x| = b/4 before the formula. The loss is in the translation, not the physics.

C1-9.8.marks: 2 marks (N25 HL, after the formula-equivalence derivation): v_max = A√(k/m), so the ratio is √2. It follows directly from ½kA² being fixed, which is why it is paired with 10A.4.

C1-9.9.marks: Markschemes accept the energy route wherever it reaches the number; the M25 HL vertical-spring item accepted three routes explicitly.

C1-10A.1.marks: 1 mark. KE maximum at equilibrium, PE maximum at the extremes, the sum constant. The Mini-Test a-t version (Q5) was answered correctly by about half.

C1-10A.2.marks: 1 mark per interval (N25 SL). Released from a compressed spring: elastic PE falls and KE rises over the first quarter; KE falls and elastic PE rises over the second. The interval wording is the new form; an answer about instants does not earn it.

C1-10A.3.marks: 2 marks (N11, M14, M15): correct substitution into E = ½mω²A², then the number; 'award 2 for a bald correct answer' is standard. Powers of ten in the amplitude are the usual loss.

C1-10A.4.marks: 2 marks (N25 HL). Any of: ω² = k/m substituted; energy at maximum displacement equated; the restoring-force equation. Quoting both forms without the link earns nothing.

C1-10A.5.marks: 1 mark, and it is the most-failed energy item on the school's tests (5 of 30 right). KE = E(1 - x²/A²) = 3E/4 at half amplitude; PE = E/4. E/4 offered as the KE is the modal wrong answer, E/2 the next.

C1-10A.6.marks: 1 mark: |x| = A/√(n + 1) where KE = nPE. The Mini-Test item was answered correctly by under half.

C1-10A.7.marks: 1 mark: four, because the condition depends on x² and is met at both signs of x on both journeys.

C1-10A.8.marks: 1 or 2 marks. x = A - d; substituting d for x is the recorded error and the item is written to catch it.

C1-10A.9.marks: 1 mark. E ∝ A²; at fixed m and A, E ∝ 1/T²; on a spring at fixed amplitude, doubling the mass leaves E = ½kA² unchanged. That last one is the single most-chosen wrong option in the school's C.1 data (20 of 30 said 2E), and the school's own key had it wrong too.

C1-10A.10.marks: 1 or 2 marks: PE an upward parabola, KE the inverted one, both meeting the flat total. See 6.5 and 6.6.

C1-10A.11.marks: 2 or 3 marks (M13, N20, N23): double frequency; always positive; correct phase (cos² for a release from rest, maxima at t = 0, T/2, T). M13 required at least one complete original oscillation for full marks; N23 required maxima to touch the other curve and minima to touch the axis. Below the axis, or repeating every T, loses the mark.

C1-10A.12.marks: 1 or 2 marks. KE = E - U then v = √(2KE/m); or T from the energy period doubled. The Mini-Test PE-x item (Q10) was answered correctly by 60 per cent.

C1-10A.13.marks: 1 mark (N25 HL). Less, and greater. See 9.4.

C1-10B.1.marks: 2 marks (M25 HL): equate weight and spring force to get e₀ = mg/k, then ½ke₀². The energy at equilibrium is not zero, and that is the whole item.

C1-10B.2.marks: 1 mark (M25 HL). Falling elastic energy means falling extension, so upward. 'Towards equilibrium' on its own was not sufficient; the markscheme wanted the extension argument.

C1-10B.3.marks: 2 marks (M25 HL). Three stores, one constant sum: elastic and kinetic can both fall while gravitational rises. The two-store SHM picture is not enough here and answers built on it lose both marks.

C1-10B.4.marks: 3 marks (M25 HL): e = √(2E/k) at each extreme, then A = e_max - e₀ (or half the difference of the extremes). Equating the elastic-energy difference to the gravitational change is an accepted alternative.

C1-10B.5.marks: Not yet a direct target. Where it appears, the mark is for the cos ωt term: ½k(e₀ + A cos ωt)² has a component at f as well as at 2f, and need not reach zero.

C1-10B.6.marks: 2 marks each (M25 HL). v_max = ωA once A is recovered. For the KE at a time, three routes were accepted: a time equation (including a phase-shifted cosine) then ½mv²; v(x) after converting extension to displacement; or full conservation across the three stores.

C1-10B.7.marks: Natural length, equilibrium extension, gravitational energy, or a graph labelled 'energy stored in the spring' mean ½ke². Displacement from equilibrium in the standard model means ½kx². Mixing them is the M25 failure mode.

C1-11.1.marks: 1 mark (multiple choice): v_max = ωA and a_max = ω²A with ω read as the coefficient of t. Two thirds of the Mini-Test candidates got it.

C1-11.2.marks: 1 mark: cos for the release from rest, sin for the start through equilibrium. Now the two special cases of x = A sin(ωt + φ).

C1-11.3.marks: 1 mark. v = 2 cos(t/3 + π/2), which is -2 sin(t/3). On the Mini-Test 12 of 15 chose 2 cos(t/3): the ω was kept and the phase constant was thrown away. That, not the ω factor, is the error to write for.

C1-11.4.marks: 1 or 2 marks. Radians throughout; a calculator in degrees loses the lot. The sign of v decides direction and speeding-up questions.

C1-11.5.marks: 1 mark. A from the peak, ω from the period, sin or cos from x(0), the sign from the initial gradient. Nearly three quarters of the Mini-Test got it; the loss is the initial condition.

C1-11.6.marks: 1 mark (N13): π/2 or 90° or a quarter of a period for x and v; π for x and a. Zero for x and a (in phase) and π/2 for x and a (the velocity value) are the distractors that work on the school's tests.

C1-11.7.marks: 1 mark for the difference (π/2 here). 2 marks for the sketch (N15): same shape and amplitude over the shown interval, then a lead or lag of the right size (1 s for π/4 at that period), consistent throughout.

C1-11.8.marks: 1 mark: Δt = (Δφ/2π)T. Usually the second half of 11.7.

C1-11.9.marks: 1 mark (the school's C1C2C5 2026 Q1, not yet in a published paper): cos φ = 0 gives π/2 or 3π/2, and the sign of v(0) = -Aω sin φ picks π/2. The quadrant is the mark; the principal value alone is the recorded slip.

C1-11.10.marks: Not yet seen as a direct target. Both branches of sin(ωt + φ) = x/A, with the sign of v selecting between them, is what a markscheme would want.

C1-11.11.marks: Phase difference is old (former 4.1). A phase-shifted equation is accepted as a method in the 2025 markschemes. No published question yet asks for an arbitrary φ as its final answer; the school's 2026 test does.

C1-12.1.marks: 2 marks (N25 1B): three periods identified, or T = 1/f; then 0.48 s. Unit not required there.

C1-12.2.marks: 3 marks (N25 1B): distance identified (14 cm); a = 2s/t²; 1.2 with m s⁻². The alternative, working from the spacing of successive oscillations with v = u + at, was capped at 2. The trace is not a graph against time, and candidates who read it as one lose the distance.

C1-12.3.marks: 1 or 2 marks: T² = 4π²m/k or T² = 4π²L/g, rearranged; ratio versions want the squares.

C1-12.4.marks: 1 mark, and it is Paper 1B's rather than C.1's: the fixed reaction-time uncertainty is a smaller fraction of a longer measured time. Here the idea only; the arithmetic is the experimental paper's.

C1-12.5.marks: 1 or 2 marks: m ∝ T², so Δm/m ≈ 2ΔT/T, and a shorter period with the same timing uncertainty gives a larger fraction. Experimental craft; C.1 supplies only the T² dependence.

C1-12.6.marks: Gradient of a-x gives -ω²; tangent to x-t gives v; gradient of v-t gives a; area under v-t gives displacement; intercepts of v-x or energy graphs give A, v_max or E; cycle count on a trace gives time.

C1-12.7.marks: 1 mark each (N25 1B): the theoretical value computed and compared numerically (1.4 against 1.2, or a percentage), the comparison consistent with the candidate's own number (ECF allowed); then a plausible cause, friction or air resistance or release conditions. 'They are different' earns nothing.

C1-12.8.marks: Convert cm, mm and ms before substitution; the Mini-Test a-x item lost two thirds of candidates to an unconverted centimetre axis. A show-that displays the equation and enough substitution to reach the quoted value. Where a markscheme allows routes, any route that reaches the number is paid.

C1-13.1.marks: 1 mark (Mini-Test, 2 of 15 right): N - mg = ±ma_max at the two extremes, so the difference is 2ma_max = 8π²mZ/T². Zero (no difference) and ma_max (one extreme instead of the difference) took six candidates each. Loss of contact is a_max = g.

C1-13.2.marks: 1 to 2 marks. Tangential (SHM) acceleration is zero at the bottom but the centripetal acceleration is not: T - mg = mv²/L, with v from energy or from v_max. The trap the marker is set for is 'zero net force at equilibrium'.

C1-13.3.marks: 1 mark each. The particle does SHM with the wave's period; the wave's own speed is a different quantity and is the wrong answer three fifths of the school's candidates gave for a particle's average speed. Counted in this document under the operation (2.4, 3.6, 9.2), not here.

C1-13.4.marks: 1 mark, rare, and a linking question in the current syllabus rather than assessed content.

C1-13.5.marks: See 1.7 and 1.8. The surrounding force calculation belongs to the other topic; the C.1 marks are for the comparison with a = -ω²x.

C1-13.6.marks: 1 to 2 marks: sinusoidal motion, one-sided output, zero for half of each cycle. The mark is for the clipping, not the sinusoid.

C1-13.7.marks: 1 mark (M25 HL): the current follows the velocity, so it is zero at the extremes and maximum through equilibrium, at the mechanical period. Faraday's law belongs to the induction topic; C.1 supplies T and the phase.

C1-13.8.marks: Decay of amplitude, damping, driven oscillation, resonance and response curves are C.4. In the magnet-coil question the SHM is C.1, the induction is another topic, and the amplitude decreasing once the coil is connected is C.4.

C1-13.9.marks: Code the subpart by what it assesses, not by the stem it sits under. A question that opens with a spring and ends in thermal physics has one or two C.1 subparts and the rest belongs elsewhere.
